header:
Date: 2026-12-22
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Sophie Kim (Redwood AE), Daniel Ortiz (Redwood SE), Liam Chen (BrightScale - Sr ML Eng), Priya Rao (BrightScale - Platform Eng), Marco Silva (BrightScale - CTO)
Notes: SE-led technical deep dive on throughput tuning: continuous batching, scheduler knobs, max_num_seqs, token limits, KV cache behavior, quantization tradeoffs, VPC/on-prem considerations.
summary: Redwood SE walked BrightScale through practical tuning steps to improve throughput while preserving tail latency. Main levers discussed: continuous batching parameters, max_num_seqs, max_tokens_per_batch, KV cache/prefix caching, scheduler prefetching and fairness knobs; also tradeoffs with quantization and VPC networking. Agreed to run benchmarks and share configs and security docs.
topics: continuous batching; scheduler knobs (max_num_seqs, max_tokens_per_batch, prefetch, fairness); token length distribution impacts; KV cache eviction/pinning; quantization (int8 vs int4) effects on throughput and quality; VPC/private deployment network considerations; benchmarking setup and metrics (tokens/sec, p50/p95 latency, GPU util)
transcript:
[00:00] Sophie Kim: hey everyone, thanks for joining, this is Sophie from Redwood, daniel's joining from our infra team, we thought we'd do a hands-on pass at throughput tuning, and, um, walk through a few knobs.

[00:18] Daniel Ortiz: hey all, hi Liam, Priya, Marco. Quick agenda: baseline numbers; continuous batching behavior; scheduler knobs like max_num_seqs and max_tokens_per_batch; kv cache/pr efixing; quant tradeoffs; benchmarking recipe. Feel free to interrupt.

[00:35] Liam Chen: thanks, yeah we're seeing pretty variable latency on our customer workloads — p95 spikes to 800ms on hosted variant, avg about 220ms, and token throughput is lower than expected. We're using a mix of short and long contexts, 20% > 1024 tokens.

[00:55] Daniel Ortiz: ok that distribution explains a lot. continuous batching in Redwood tries to fill batches up to either max_num_seqs or max_tokens_per_batch, whichever comes first. So with a heavy tail of long sequences you often hit max_tokens_per_batch early and get small batch sizes for short requests behind long ones.

[01:12] Priya Rao: can you repeat the two limits? max_num_seqs vs max_tokens_per_batch?

[01:17] Daniel Ortiz: sure — max_num_seqs is the max number of concurrent sequences the scheduler will pack into a single execution. max_tokens_per_batch is a tokens cap to avoid OOM or excessive latency when someone sends many long contexts. For example if max_num_seqs=16 but max_tokens_per_batch=8192, then a batch of 4 long 4096-token sequences would hit the token cap and run early.

[01:40] Marco Silva: so what's a safe starting point?

[01:43] Daniel Ortiz: safe start depends on the model and GPU. For g5-series gpus with a 40GB memory budget and quantized int8 models, we've seen stable sweet spots: max_num_seqs between 6–12 for long-tail workloads. For mixed workloads start with 8. max_tokens_per_batch you can set to 16k for 8k token max per request, or set it relative to avg sequence length.

[02:05] Liam Chen: our current config is max_num_seqs: 32, max_tokens_per_batch: 16384 — might be too permissive?

[02:12] Daniel Ortiz: yeah that 32 is high; it lets the scheduler overpack short queries which increases latency variance because long ones dominate the GPU execution time. Lowering to 8 will improve p95 in mixed loads but could reduce peak throughput for purely short sequences. It's a tradeoff.

[02:34] Sophie Kim: also important: continuous batching has an idle timer — if you set the batching window too large you'll increase latency. We usually recommend a small batching window (2–5ms) with max_num_seqs tuned to your workload.

[02:50] Priya Rao: can we control fairness? We don't want a few long requests to block many short ones.

[02:55] Daniel Ortiz: yes, Redwood supports fairness/scheduling priorities. There's a preemptive path — you can mark short, latency-sensitive routes with higher priority. Scheduler knob 'fairness_threshold' (mis-transcribed earlier in docs as 'fairness_throttle') will cause the scheduler to flush batches early if latency-sensitive requests are queued. I can share the exact YAML.

[03:20] Liam Chen: what about kv cache? we're doing chat-style convos with prefix caching but we notice cache misses sometimes and eviction.

[03:27] Daniel Ortiz: kv cache is per-model + per-session by default. Two things: prefix caching (pinned prefixes) and TTL/eviction. For throughput you want to pin the common prefixes (prompts) to avoid re-encoding. Also there's a 'kv_cache_capacity' per instance — if you set that too low the cache evicts and causes rework. For high-concurrency, increase kv_cache_capacity and consider sharding the cache across workers.

[03:52] Marco Silva: any gotchas with private deployments and the KV cache?

[03:56] Daniel Ortiz: networking can bite you — if your VPC has limited bandwidth between the control plane and workers you'll see increased RPC latency on cache misses. For on-prem we recommend co-locating the cache layer with the inference nodes; avoid cross-subnet chatter. Also ensure MTU and jumbo frames are consistent, otherwise packetization increases CPU overhead.

[04:18] Priya Rao: quantization — we tried int4 and saw some quality degradation, but huge gains in throughput. What's the recommended approach?

[04:25] Daniel Ortiz: yep int4 gives great throughput but can impact some LLMs more than others. Practical approach: run a small eval set and measure quality regression. Then use mixed-precision: int8 for attention/kernels and fp16 for some sensitive ops if the runtime supports it. Redwood Optimize can suggest quantization profiles per model and workload — we'll share the recommendations.

[04:50] Sophie Kim: quick interruption — I posted the benchmark sheet: https://redwood.example.com/benchmarks/brightscale-spike (note: link placeholder) and the scheduler config gist: https://redwood.example.com/configs/scheduler-template.

[05:05] Liam Chen: thanks, saw it. For benchmarks, do you recommend synthetic load or replayed traffic?

[05:10] Daniel Ortiz: replayed traffic is best for tail latency; synthetic can help isolate factors. For throughput tuning run 3 buckets: short-only, long-only, and mixed (reflecting your real distribution). Track tokens/sec, GPU util, p50/p95/p99 latency, and batch fill rates.

[05:35] Priya Rao: how do we read the batch fill metrics?

[05:38] Daniel Ortiz: batch fill shows average seqs per execution and tokens per execution. If seqs/execution is low for short requests consider increasing batching window slightly; if tokens/execution is hitting the token cap frequently then lower max_num_seqs or raise max_tokens_per_batch if memory allows.

[06:00] Marco Silva: is there a dynamic approach? We don't want to manually tune per-workload all the time.

[06:05] Daniel Ortiz: yes we have an adaptive scheduler option — it'll adjust max_num_seqs based on recent latency/throughput signals, but we advise using it after you've established safe bounds. Adaptive is conservative: it won't exceed configured max_num_seqs and respects token caps. The trick is to set upper/lower bounds.

[06:25] Liam Chen: what about the scheduler prefetch or pipeline depth? I remember a knob called prefetch_count?

[06:30] Daniel Ortiz: prefetch_count controls how many sequence frames the scheduler pulls ahead into the GPU queue; increasing it can boost throughput at the cost of memory and some latency. For large models on 80GB GPUs you can raise it; for 40GB start conservative. Also watch GPU util and CPU overhead — prefetching too much increases memory pressure and might reduce throughput if it causes swapping.

[06:52] Sophie Kim: do you have constraints on token limits per request? BrightScale mentioned 8k token max — is that ok?

[06:58] Daniel Ortiz: 8k is fine if you tune max_tokens_per_batch accordingly and use prefix caching. For 8k requests you may want max_tokens_per_batch >= 32k so a couple of long sequences can co-exist in the same batch if desired; but that will increase memory usage. Often we keep max_tokens_per_batch at 16k and let long requests run solo to keep latency bounded.

[07:20] Priya Rao: any specific numbers we should watch for on GPU util?

[07:23] Daniel Ortiz: aim for sustained 70–90% GPU util for cost efficiency. If you see 30–50% with high p95 latency, that's a sign of batching inefficiency (too many small or fragmented batches). If you see 95%+ and rising latency, you might be over-subscribing memory.

[07:40] Liam Chen: can Redwood handle per-route config? We have one route latency sensitive, others throughput-first.

[07:45] Daniel Ortiz: yes, route-level configs are supported. You can pin different schedulers or priority tags per route. E.g., set route A with priority high, max_num_seqs=4, batching_window=3ms, and route B with max_num_seqs=12, batching_window=10ms. That way latency-sensitive traffic doesn't get stuck behind heavy batches.

[08:05] Marco Silva: curious about failure modes — if we lower max_num_seqs aggressively do we risk losing throughput?

[08:10] Daniel Ortiz: yes, lowering max_num_seqs reduces max theoretical throughput since you're limiting batch parallelism. The key is to find the knee where p95 improves with minimal drop in tokens/sec. That's why the sweep is important.

[08:24] Sophie Kim: quick practical example — set up a sweep: max_num_seqs [4,8,12], max_tokens_per_batch [8192,16384,32768], batching_window [3ms,8ms]. Run 30-minute runs for each combo with mixed traffic. Collect p50/p95 tokens/sec and batch_fill. Daniel will help automate that.

[08:45] Daniel Ortiz: yep I'll share a script to parametrize this and upload results to the benchmark sheet. We'll also hook GPU traces to see kernel saturation and KV cache hit/miss rate.

[09:00] Priya Rao: about KV cache hits — what's a good hit rate?

[09:03] Daniel Ortiz: for chat apps we aim for >85% hit rate on pinned prefixes; lower than 70% means you're re-encoding too often. If hits are low, check session affinity — requests should route to the same worker if they share KV. If you're on a multi-tenant cluster with autoscaling, ensure sticky routing or a shared external cache.

[09:24] Liam Chen: sticky routing could be a problem in our k8s autoscaler — how do we ensure affinity?

[09:28] Daniel Ortiz: use session affinity via consistent hashing on session id at the fronting proxy, or use our session-store backed by Redis for cross-node KV cache retrieval. For private deployments, co-locating Redis/Cache within same network reduces latency.

[09:45] Marco Silva: security and VPC — anything we should watch when moving to private?

[09:49] Sophie Kim: we cover this in the security pack but high level: SAML/SSO, KMS integration for key management, audit logs, and network egress restrictions. For KV cache and model artifacts, ensure S3 or object store permissions are locked down and the nodes have restricted IAM roles. We'll attach the SOC2 docs.

[10:10] Priya Rao: back to quantization — you mentioned mixed-precision earlier, any runtime flags?

[10:14] Daniel Ortiz: runtime flag 'quant_profile' can be set to int8-mixed or int4-fast, and 'sensitivity_eval' enables per-layer checks during model load to warn about risky ops. Use sensitivity_eval in staging runs.

[10:30] Liam Chen: what about kernel selection and compilation — do we need to recompile for different quant profiles?

[10:34] Daniel Ortiz: yes, the runtime selects kernels at model load. Changing quant profiles may trigger different kernels and an initial warmup compile step; expect a small warmup latency spike when you flip profiles. We recommend doing that during off hours.

[10:50] Sophie Kim: let's walk through an example config recommended for BrightScale mixed workload — Daniel?

[10:55] Daniel Ortiz: recommended starter config: 
- max_num_seqs: 8
- max_tokens_per_batch: 16384
- batching_window_ms: 5
- fairness_threshold: 0.6 (this is normalized; forces early flush if short queue is waiting)
- kv_cache_capacity: 20000 entries per worker (adjust by session/profile)
- quant_profile: int8-mixed for baseline, run sensitivity eval for int4.

[11:25] Priya Rao: acceptable defaults. We'll trial that. For on-prem, any infra sizing guidance?

[11:29] Daniel Ortiz: for mixed loads and 8k tokens max, we suggest 80GB GPUs for headroom if you expect many concurrent long sequences. For cost reasons, 40GB with tuned batching works if you cap concurrent long sequences. Also configure autoscaler thresholds to maintain target GPU util ~75%.

[11:50] Marco Silva: can Redwood help run the initial benchmarks?

[11:53] Sophie Kim: yes we offer a Managed Spike run; Daniel will run a 1-hour spike and we'll provide telemetry. That was one of the action items.

[12:05] Liam Chen: what telemetry will you need from us?

[12:08] Daniel Ortiz: token length histograms (per-route), p95 SLA targets, model name and quantization profile, and example prompts for pinned prefixes. Send those and I'll configure the script.

[12:20] Priya Rao: about pinned prefixes — is that manual?

[12:23] Daniel Ortiz: you annotate routes with 'pin_prefix=true' and provide a list of common prompts; runtime will keep the KV cached for those. There's also an auto-detect mode but it's conservative.

[12:35] Sophie Kim: small digression — customers sometimes run into noisy neighbor issues on shared Dedicated pools, how do you avoid that?

[12:42] Daniel Ortiz: use HW isolation (dedicated capacity) for heavy workloads, or strict per-customer quotas and priority. Also our smart routing can move noisy clients to preemptible nodes.

[12:55] Marco Silva: any notes on network egress costs for larger batch sizes?

[12:58] Daniel Ortiz: egress is mostly for logs and artifacts; tokens are internal. But if you stream a lot of tokens out per request you might see bandwidth usage; streaming in small chunks reduces memory but increases RPC overhead. Balance depends on your topology.

[13:15] Liam Chen: can we get example metrics thresholds to decide when to increase max_num_seqs?

[13:20] Daniel Ortiz: sure — if p95 latency < target and GPU util < 80% and batch_fill < 60% then increasing max_num_seqs by 2 is reasonable. If p95 exceeds target, back off. We'll include a decision tree in the doc.

[13:40] Priya Rao: earlier you mentioned preemptive path for short requests — how does that affect token accounting?

[13:45] Daniel Ortiz: accounting is per-execution so short requests that preempt still consume tokens as normal; however, they may reduce batching efficiency slightly. The tradeoff is improved tail latency for latency-sensitive routes.

[14:00] Sophie Kim: quick check — any regulatory or security concerns with pinned prefixes? They may contain PII in some cases.

[14:05] Daniel Ortiz: good point. We recommend masking or hashing sensitive prefixes before pinning, or using per-customer encrypted caches (KMS-backed). We'll include the encryption and audit-log guidance in the security pack.

[14:25] Marco Silva: ok what's realistic p95 improvement we might see from tuning?

[14:28] Daniel Ortiz: for mixed workloads we've seen p95 drop from ~800ms to ~250–350ms after tuning batching and enabling prefix pinning. Tokens/sec usually improves or stays roughly the same. In some cases throughput drops slightly but tail latency improves significantly.

[14:48] Liam Chen: great. Let's talk about next steps and ownership.

[14:52] Sophie Kim: recap: Daniel will run the initial 1-hour benchmark with our scripts using the starter config and sweep a few knobs; Liam will share traffic profile and target SLAs; Sophie will send the security docs and scheduler YAML; follow-up in two weeks.

[15:10] Priya Rao: one more small question — we use an ingress that does rate limiting per user, will that interact with batching?

[15:15] Daniel Ortiz: rate limiting upstream can fragment batches if it's applied per-connection; consider applying rate limits at route-level after the batching proxy, or use token-bucket on the gateway that allows bursts within the batching window. We can help with config examples.

[15:32] Marco Silva: ok thanks everyone, that was super helpful.

[15:36] Sophie Kim: thanks, we'll get the docs and scripts out today. Any final questions?

[15:45] Liam Chen: none from me. Looking forward to the spike.

[15:48] Sophie Kim: thanks all — I'll send meeting notes, action items, and links. Talk soon.

[15:55] End of recording.

Notes about transcript: occasional ASR errors present (e.g., "preemptive path" heard as "premptive pass", "KV cache" sometimes split into "K V cache"). Some speaker labels are paraphrased.
